usage: Standalone color noun; works as 'the purple one' in shops
Color noun directly modifies the next noun — no particle, no -ㄴ ending
연- (薄, 'thin/pale') prefix makes any color softer
I'll take the purple one, please
-(으)로 = 'in/by that color', the natural way to pick a color
examples: 저는 보라색을 제일 좋아해요.
Purple is my favorite color.
색 + 을/를 좋아해요 names a favorite; note Korean makes 'purple' the object, not the subject
이 티셔츠 보라색도 있어요?
Does this T-shirt also come in purple?
-도 ('also') is the shopping reflex for asking about another color option
보라색이랑 분홍색 중에 뭐가 더 나아요?
Between the purple and the pink, which is better?
N이랑 N 중에 = 'among these listed', casual spoken comparison
nuance: 보라색 is the general cover-word for the whole purple range. The 색 part is the Sino-Korean 色 ('color') glued onto the native root 보라, so almost every Korean color noun is '[root] + 색'. The dividing line with neighbours matters: 자주색 (紫朱色) leans into a deep reddish wine-purple, while 연보라색 is the pale lilac on cosmetics and stationery, and crucially 보라색 is NOT a shade of 파란색 (blue) — Korean treats purple and blue as fully separate basic colors, unlike the loose English habit of calling things 'blue-ish purple'. Register is neutral: 보라색 is fine in any setting. The classic English-speaker pitfall is grammar, not vocabulary: you do not say 보라색은 가방 ('purple-TOPIC bag'); the color noun sits bare right in front — 보라색 가방. Treat 보라색 like an adjective-noun in English ('purple bag') and just stack the two nouns.

usage: Native-rooted standard word; the loanword 핑크 is equally common
Color noun stacks straight onto the noun it describes
연- (薄) = pale; opposite vibe from 형광 핑크 (neon pink)
Got a color other than pink?
N 말고 = 'not N (but something else)', asking for an alternative
examples: 벚꽃이 분홍색이라서 진짜 예뻐요.
The cherry blossoms are pink, so they're really pretty.
이라서 = 'because it IS (a color)'; this -이라서 form is for nouns
딸 방을 분홍색으로 칠했어요.
I painted my daughter's room pink.
색으로 칠하다 = 'paint (it) a color'; the -(으)로 marks the resulting color
분홍색보다 빨간색이 더 잘 어울려요.
Red suits you better than pink.
N보다 더 = comparison; 어울리다 = 'suits', a high-frequency clothing verb
nuance: 분홍색 is the everyday word for pink and trades places freely with the English loanword 핑크, which sounds a touch trendier in fashion and beauty talk (립스틱 색, 네일). The first half 분홍 is itself Sino-Korean (粉紅, literally 'powder-red'), so the word's own history already says 'pinkish red' — which is exactly why the key boundary is with 빨간색 (red): pink is a separate color noun, not 'light red', and Koreans will not understand 연한 빨간색 as 'pink'. Tone-wise the word carries no built-in 'girly' baggage; the vibe comes from the shade — soft 연분홍색 vs loud 형광 핑크 (neon pink). The English-speaker pitfall is two-pronged: don't reach for 빨간색 to mean pink, and remember the 'because it is' reason form for a noun is N이라서 / N이어서 (분홍색이라서), never the verb-style 분홍색해서.

usage: Everyday neutral; extremely common for clothing
Color + clothing item, a staple combo in real speech
계열 (系列) = 'lineage of colors', used when matching outfits
examples: 오늘 하늘이 회색이라 비 올 것 같아요.
The sky is gray today, so it looks like it'll rain.
올 것 같아요 = 'looks like it will', a soft guess
회색 정장이 제일 무난해요.
A gray suit is the safest choice.
무난하다 = 'safe/inoffensive', the go-to clothing compliment
회색이랑 검은색 중에 뭐 살까요?
Which should I buy, gray or black?
-ㄹ까요? asks the listener to weigh in on a decision
nuance: 회색 is the default neutral of Korean wardrobes and interiors, so often it gets the praise 무난하다 ('safe, fail-proof, won't clash'). The 회 here is Sino-Korean 灰 ('ash'), so the word literally means 'ash-color' — a useful memory hook and a reminder that, like English, Korean stretches 회색 figuratively to an overcast mood or a dreary 'gray' day. Shades split into 연회색 (light gray) and 진회색 or the loanword 차콜 (charcoal). Two pitfalls hit English speakers. First, pronunciation: 회 is a single rounded 'hwe' syllable (close to 'hweh'), not 'hoe-ee' in two beats. Second, category: 회색 is its own neutral, NOT a kind of 흰색/하얀색 (white) — saying 밝은 흰색 won't mean 'light gray'; use 연회색.

usage: All-purpose brown: hair, leather, wood, coffee
The default way to describe brown hair
진- (津) = darker; the safe word for very dark brown hair (not 검은색)
밝은 ('bright/light') + color; common at the hair salon
examples: 머리를 갈색으로 염색했어요.
I dyed my hair brown.
색으로 염색하다 = 'dye (it) a color'; -(으)로 marks the new color
갈색 구두가 이 바지랑 잘 어울려요.
Brown shoes go well with these pants.
N(이)랑 잘 어울리다 = 'goes well with N'
원두를 볶으면 갈색이 돼요.
When you roast coffee beans, they turn brown.
색이 되다 = 'become/turn (a color)'; 색을 되다 is wrong
nuance: 갈색 is your default, all-purpose brown for hair, leather, wood, and coffee. The 갈 is Sino-Korean 褐 ('brown, coarse cloth'), so it's literally 'brown-color', and it sits in the medium-to-dark band of the brown range. Know its two neighbours: 밤색 (栗色, 'chestnut-color') specifically names a warm reddish-brown loved for hair and shoes, and for pale tan tones people borrow 베이지(색) instead. The big English-speaker pitfalls are at the dark and light edges. At the dark end, very dark brown hair is 진갈색, not 검은색 (black) — Koreans hear those as different colors. At the light end, blonde is NOT 노란색 (yellow); it's 금발 (金髮, 'gold-hair') for the hair itself or 밝은 갈색 for dyed light-brown. Grammar-wise, use 갈색이 되다 ('become brown'), since 되다 takes the subject particle 이/가, not 을/를.

usage: The dark end of blue; standard in suits and uniforms
네이비 swaps in freely in fashion contexts
계열 (系列) = color family, used when matching pieces
examples: 면접 때는 남색 정장이 무난해요.
A navy suit is a safe choice for an interview.
N 때(는) = 'when it comes to (the occasion of) N'
이 가방 검은색 말고 남색으로 살래요.
I'll buy this bag in navy, not black.
N 말고 = 'not N (but ~)', swapping the chosen option
남색이 파란색보다 더 차분해 보여요.
Navy looks more composed than blue.
더 ~ 보여요 = 'looks more ~'; 차분하다 = calm/subdued
nuance: 남색 is the deep, near-ink blue of school uniforms, business suits, and dark denim. The 남 is Sino-Korean 藍 ('indigo', the dye plant), so the word literally means 'indigo-color' — a good reminder that it lives at the DARK end of blue, the opposite pole from 하늘색 (sky blue). Against everyday 파란색 (a saturated mid-blue), 남색 reads as more formal and 차분하다 ('calm, composed'), which is exactly why it dominates uniforms and interview wear; younger shoppers often just say the loanword 네이비. Two English-speaker pitfalls: first, don't merge 남색 with 파란색 — they are not interchangeable, and a navy suit described as 파란색 정장 will sound like a bright-blue suit. Second, when stating 'navy is more X', the comparison particle goes on the thing you compare against: 남색이 파란색보다 (navy, compared-to blue), not 남색보다 파란색이 unless you mean the reverse.

usage: Native compound 하늘(sky)+색(color); the standard word for light blue
Do you have it in sky blue too?
-도 asks about one more color option at a shop
examples: 저 벽 색깔이 하늘색이에요.
That wall is sky blue.
N이에요 states the color as a predicate; 하늘색 ends in a consonant (ㄱ), so it takes 이에요, not 예요
여름엔 하늘색 셔츠가 시원해 보여요.
In summer a light-blue shirt looks refreshing.
시원해 보이다 = 'looks cool/refreshing'; common summer praise
아기 옷은 하늘색이 인기가 많아요.
Sky blue is very popular for baby clothes.
인기가 많다 = 'is very popular'; 인기가 있다 also works
nuance: 하늘색 is the soft, pale blue of a clear sky, and unlike most color words its first half is the native noun 하늘 ('sky'), not a Sino-Korean root — so it's literally 'sky-color', a perfect built-in mnemonic. It reads as fresh, clean, and 시원하다 ('cool/refreshing'), which is why it's a summer-shirt and baby-clothes favorite, and it sits at the pale end opposite deep 남색 (navy); even against plain 파란색 (a stronger mid-blue) it stays clearly lighter. The sharp English-speaker pitfall is mixing up the color name with the thing: 하늘색 is the COLOR 'sky blue', while 하늘 is the actual sky. So a clear sky is 하늘이 맑아요 ('the sky is clear'), never 하늘색이 맑아요. Also resist flattening it to 파란색 — Koreans firmly separate pale 하늘색 from saturated 파란색, so 'light blue' should be 하늘색.

usage: Everyday native word for a circle (vs. formal 원)
그리다 = 'draw', the natural verb for shapes on paper
to circle / mark with a circle
치다 here = 'put/strike a mark', a fixed collocation
On tests a 동그라미 means 'correct', the Korean 'O'
examples: 정답에 동그라미를 치세요.
Circle the correct answer.
N에 동그라미를 치다 = 'put a circle ON N'; the surface takes 에
아이가 종이에 동그라미를 그렸어요.
The child drew a circle on the paper.
그리다 (draw) vs 치다 (mark): drawing a shape uses 그리다
맞으면 동그라미, 틀리면 가위표예요.
Circle if right, X if wrong.
가위표 ('scissor mark', X) is the partner of 동그라미
nuance: 동그라미 is the warm, everyday native word for a circle (built on the adjective 동그랗다, 'round'), while 원 (圓, 'circle') is the formal/mathematical term you'd meet in geometry class — so a kid draws a 동그라미 but a textbook discusses 원의 넓이 ('the area of a circle'). The big cultural pitfall for English speakers is the GRADING SYSTEM: in Korea a 동그라미 (O) means 'correct' and an X (called 가위표 or 엑스) means 'wrong' — the O/X habit, not the American check-and-cross, so a circle here is never a neutral doodle but a clear 'yes/right'. Watch the two different verbs and particles: you 그리다 ('draw') a circle as a shape, but you 치다 ('mark') a circle onto an answer, and the thing you mark on takes 에 (정답에 동그라미를 치다).

usage: Casual native word for a triangle (vs. formal 삼각형)
모양 ('shape') attaches to the shape word
examples: 김밥을 세모 모양으로 잘랐어요.
I cut the gimbap into triangle shapes.
모양으로 자르다 = 'cut INTO a (shape)'; -(으)로 marks the resulting form
이 표지판은 세모라서 경고 표지판이에요.
This sign is a triangle, so it's a warning sign.
N(이)라서 = 'because it IS (a noun)'
맞으면 동그라미, 애매하면 세모 치세요.
Circle if right, triangle if it's iffy.
애매하다 = 'vague/borderline'; here 세모 (마크를) 치다 is shortened
nuance: 세모 is the friendly, kid-and-everyday word for a triangle, while 삼각형 (三角形, literally 'three-corner-shape') is reserved for math class and formal writing — the 모 in 세모/네모 is a native morpheme meaning 'corner/edge', so 세모 is intuitively 'three-corner'. As a GRADING mark, 세모 carries a specific meaning English speakers won't guess: it means 'partially correct / so-so', sitting between 동그라미 (fully correct) and the X (wrong), so a teacher's triangle on your work is 'half credit', not a shape doodle. Two pitfalls: don't default to 삼각형 in casual talk (it sounds like a math lecture), and the word stays just 세모 — there's no 세모형; the '-형' (形) ending belongs only to the formal 삼각형.

Two pitfalls: don't default to 삼각형 in casual talk (it sounds like a math lecture), and the word stays just 세모 — there's no 세모형; the '-형' (形) ending belongs only to the formal 삼각형.

mistakes: Defaulting to 삼각형 in casual conversation — for a simple everyday triangle people say 세모; 삼각형 sounds textbook-formal.
Inventing 세모형 by adding -형 — the casual word is just 세모; the -형 (形) ending belongs to the formal 삼각형 only.
Misreading a 세모 grading mark as 'wrong' — it signals 'partially right / borderline', between 동그라미 (correct) and X (wrong).

usage: Casual native word; covers both square and rectangle
From 네모나다 → 네모난 + noun, e.g. 네모난 상자
칸 = a cell on a form or grid
examples: 네모 칸 안에 이름을 쓰세요.
Write your name inside the box.
N 안에 = 'inside N'; 칸 is the fill-in cell
창문이 네모 모양이에요.
The window is square/rectangular.
N 모양이에요 = 'is (a certain) shape'
네모난 접시에 담으니까 더 예뻐요.
Plated on a square dish, it looks nicer.
네모난 + noun uses the adjective form; 담다 = 'to plate/put in'
nuance: 네모 is the casual native word that loosely covers BOTH squares and rectangles — like 세모, its 모 means 'corner', so 네모 is intuitively 'four-corner'. When you must be precise, the math terms split it: 정사각형 (正四角形, 'regular four-corner-shape') is a true square and 직사각형 (直四角形, 'right-angle four-corner-shape') is a rectangle. The most useful thing for English speakers is the ADJECTIVE: 네모 has the descriptive verb 네모나다, whose modifier form is 네모난 (네모난 상자, 'a boxy box') — there is no 네모적인 or 네모스러운; learners over-applying the Sino-Korean '-적' suffix get it wrong here. Also note 네모 칸 is the everyday term for a fill-in box on a form, so 'write it in the box' is 네모 칸에 쓰다, where the box takes 에 (or 안에 for 'inside').

Saying 네모를 쓰다 for 'fill in the box' — you write IN it: 네모 칸에 쓰다 (or 네모 칸 안에 쓰다).

usage: Pattern noun stacks onto the clothing item
examples: 줄무늬 티셔츠가 깔끔해 보여요.
The striped T-shirt looks neat.
깔끔해 보이다 = 'looks tidy/clean'
저는 무늬 없는 옷보다 줄무늬가 좋아요.
I prefer striped clothes to plain ones.
무늬 없는 = 'patternless/plain'; N보다 N이 좋다 = prefer
세로 줄무늬가 키가 커 보이게 해요.
Vertical stripes make you look taller.
키가 커 보이게 하다 = 'make (you) look taller'
nuance: 줄무늬 is a transparent native compound: 줄 ('line/cord') + 무늬 ('pattern, decorative design'), so it's literally 'line-pattern'. The base 무늬 is the general word for ANY surface pattern, which is the key to a whole family — 체크무늬 (check), 물방울무늬 (polka dot), 꽃무늬 (floral), 줄무늬 (stripe) — and that's why dropping 무늬 changes the meaning: bare 줄 just means 'a line/string', not the patterned look, so a 'striped shirt' must be 줄무늬 셔츠, not 줄 셔츠. Koreans casually pin down direction with 가로 ('horizontal') vs 세로 ('vertical') when it matters for fashion. The standout English-speaker pitfall is pronunciation: 무늬 is pronounced like '무니' (the ㅢ after a consonant collapses to ㅣ), so 줄무늬 sounds like 'jul-mu-ni', never 'mu-nui'.

mistakes: Saying just 줄 for a striped pattern — bare 줄 means 'a line/string'; the pattern word needs 무늬, i.e. 줄무늬.

Translating 'striped' with an adjective form like 줄무늬적인 — Korean just stacks the pattern noun: 줄무늬 셔츠.

usage: Very common in casual fall/winter fashion
패턴 (loanword) also works in fashion talk
examples: 가을에는 체크무늬 셔츠가 잘 어울려요.
Plaid shirts suit the fall season well.
N에는 = 'in/during N (as the topic)'
체크무늬 스커트 하나 살까 봐요.
I'm thinking of buying a plaid skirt.
-ㄹ까 봐요 here = 'I'm thinking I might ~' (a leaning intention)
이 식당은 체크무늬 식탁보를 써요.
This restaurant uses checkered tablecloths.
식탁보 = 'tablecloth'; 쓰다 = 'use'
nuance: 체크무늬 is a hybrid word — the English loan 체크 ('check') plus native 무늬 ('pattern') — and it covers the whole checked family from fine gingham to tartan plaid (Korean doesn't split 'plaid' vs 'check' the way English does). It leans warm and casual, strongly tied to autumn/winter clothing (flannel shirts, mufflers) and cozy homeware (blankets, tablecloths). The sharpest English-speaker pitfall is the 체크 homonym trap: 체크무늬 is the PATTERN, but 체크(하다) means 'to check/verify/tick' something entirely — so 이거 체크해 주세요 means 'please check (verify) this', never 'make this plaid'. Also, as with all pattern words, keep the 무늬: drop it and 체크 alone tilts toward the 'verify' meaning, so for the fabric look use the full 체크무늬 (or 체크 패턴).

mistakes: Using bare 체크 for the fabric pattern in careful speech — 체크 alone often reads as 'check/verify'; the pattern noun is 체크무늬 (or 체크 패턴).
Confusing 체크무늬 (the pattern) with 체크(하다) ('to check/verify/tick') — 이거 체크해 주세요 means 'please verify this', not anything about plaid.
Splitting 'plaid' from 'check' — Korean 체크무늬 covers both gingham and tartan, so don't hunt for a separate word for 'plaid'.

usage: 땡땡이 is the colloquial nickname for the dots
examples: 물방울무늬 원피스가 귀여워요.
The polka-dot dress is cute.
귀엽다 = 'cute', the typical read on this pattern
우산에 물방울무늬가 있어서 비 올 때 잘 어울려요.
The umbrella has polka dots, so it suits rainy days.
N이/가 있어서 = 'because there is N'
요즘은 땡땡이무늬라고도 많이 해요.
These days people often call it 'ttaengttaeng-i' dots too.
N(이)라고(도) 하다 = '(also) call it N'
nuance: 물방울무늬 is the textbook word for polka dots, literally 'water-drop pattern' (물방울 'water drop' + 무늬 'pattern'), since each round dot looks like a droplet. In casual speech, though, most Koreans say 땡땡이(무늬), an onomatopoeic nickname (originally from Japanese 点々 'dots'), so recognizing both registers matters: 물방울무늬 is the neutral/written form, 땡땡이무늬 the everyday spoken one. The pattern reads as retro and 귀엽다 ('cute'), popular on dresses, blouses, and umbrellas. Two English-speaker pitfalls: don't calque polka dots as 점무늬 ('dot-pattern') — it's understandable but not what people actually say; use 물방울무늬 or 땡땡이무늬. And keep the 무늬: bare 물방울 means a single literal water drop, so 'a polka-dot dress' is 물방울무늬 원피스, not 물방울 원피스.

mistakes: Calquing polka dots as 점무늬 ('dot-pattern') — it's understandable but unnatural; say 물방울무늬 or casual 땡땡이무늬.
Dropping 무늬 and saying only 물방울 — that means a single water drop, not the pattern; the pattern is 물방울무늬.
Treating 땡땡이무늬 as wrong or slangy-bad — it's the normal everyday spoken form, just less formal than 물방울무늬.

usage: Conversational and vivid; especially natural for hair, shoes, bags, and animals
Color noun directly before the noun — no particle between them
A neutral synonym; slightly more dictionary-like than 까만색
I'll take the black one, please
-(으)로 marks the chosen color in shopping
examples: 저는 까만색 가방을 자주 써요.
I often use a black bag.
Color noun + object; no particle between 까만색 and 가방
까만색이랑 검은색은 둘 다 자연스러워요.
Both kkaman-saek and geomeun-saek sound natural.
Learners should recognize both black words
까만색 말고 회색도 있어요?
Do you have gray too, not black?
N 말고 = 'not N, but another option'
nuance: 까만색 is the vivid, everyday color noun for black. It comes from 까맣다, so it feels a little more visual and conversational than 검은색, which is the more neutral dictionary-like color noun. In shopping, clothing, and simple descriptions, both are safe: 까만색 가방 and 검은색 가방 are both natural. The important grammar point is that Korean color nouns sit right before the noun they describe, with no particle in between — 까만색 신발, not 까만색의 신발 or 까만색은 신발. English speakers also overuse 검은색 because it looks tidier in dictionaries; that is fine, but learners should not be surprised when native speakers casually say 까만색.

structuredNuance.t: 까만색 is the vivid, everyday color noun for black. It is natural for hair, shoes, bags, clothes, animals, and simple shopping choices.
검은색 is a neutral synonym and sounds a little more dictionary-like. 까만색 feels more visual and conversational because it comes from 까맣다.
Do not put a particle between the color and the noun. Say 까만색 가방 or 검은색 신발, not 까만색은 가방 or 까만색의 가방.

mistakes: Adding a particle between the color and noun — for 'a black bag' say 까만색 가방, not 까만색은 가방.
Thinking 검은색 is the only correct word for black — 까만색 is common and natural in everyday speech.
Using 까맣다 as if it were the noun color in shopping — 까맣다 is the adjective; the color noun is 까만색.

usage: Color noun stacks directly before clothing
Loanword-flavored synonym, common in fashion and products
examples: 주황색 우산이 눈에 잘 띄어요.
The orange umbrella stands out well.
눈에 띄다 = to catch the eye / stand out
이 색은 노란색보다 주황색에 가까워요.
This color is closer to orange than yellow.
N에 가깝다 = to be close to N
주황색 말고 빨간색도 있어요?
Do you have red too, not orange?
N 말고 asks for another option
nuance: 주황색 is the standard Korean color noun for orange. It sits between 빨간색 and 노란색, and it is common for clothes, traffic cones, fruit packaging, stationery, and bright signs. 오렌지색 also works, especially in fashion, cosmetics, and product listings, but 주황색 is the safest school/dictionary form. The main learner trap is category drift: Korean speakers will not usually call orange simply 노란색 or 빨간색 unless the shade truly leans that way. Grammatically, treat it like the other color nouns: 주황색 우산, 주황색 티셔츠, 주황색으로 주세요.

Do not flatten orange into yellow or red. If the color is orange, use 주황색 or 오렌지색, then place it directly before the noun: 주황색 우산.
